bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Commodity price volatility (LME lead, copper, aluminium) — MD&A 'Market and Financial' risk: fluctuations in global market prices for lead, copper and aluminium directly impact revenue and gross margins. Mitigation is a disciplined LME hedging mechanism with sales prices monitored against raw-material procurement. The structural exposure is visible in management's own Q4 commentary (sibling bundles): a short-window surge in LME copper compressed realisations because the industry's formula-based pricing expresses price as a percentage of LME.
- Raw material insecurity - dependence on scrap availability — MD&A 'Operational' risk: dependence on scrap availability, both domestic and imported, heightens sensitivity to supply-side disruption, quality variation, logistics delays and price volatility. Mitigated by a diversified sourcing network; domestic sourcing was raised to approximately 39% of volume during the year to cut dependence on long-lead-time imports. The remaining ~61% import dependence is the structural residue.
- Foreign exchange exposure — MD&A 'Market and Financial' risk: significant international trade in US Dollars and Euros creates currency risk. Managed by monitoring net exposures and using forward contracts, with a partial natural hedge to the extent import and export flows align.
- Operational safety in molten-metal and hazardous-material handling — MD&A 'Operational' risk and the top-ranked BRSR material issue: recycling, smelting, refining and handling of molten metals are safety-sensitive; recycling operations involve heavy machinery and hazardous materials posing injury risk to the workforce. Stated financial implication is negative - potential medical compensation, legal costs and operational downtime. Mitigated by safety policies, risk assessments, safety manuals, PPE, mandatory training and ISO 45001:2018 certification.
- Geopolitical instability, shipping-route and trade disruption — MD&A 'Strategic and External' risk: conflicts, trade policy changes, port disruptions or restrictions in key sourcing and export regions can affect procurement, logistics and market access. This risk has already crystallised twice in the year on management's own account - a freight/logistics cost spike on import containers, and delay to the Kuwait (Abraj Al Khaleej) project timeline.
- Working capital intensity — MD&A 'Financial' risk: timely scrap procurement, inventory holding, receivables management and funding support are critical in a volatile commodity environment. Managed through internal controls, treasury processes and management review. Structurally amplified by global sourcing, commodity-linked pricing and the working-capital-intensive nature of recycling.
- Environmental and EPR regulatory compliance, and GHG/energy intensity — MD&A 'Regulatory and ESG' risk (mitigation text TRUNCATED mid-sentence at 'The Company' in the routed extract) plus BRSR material issue #2: energy-intensive recycling processes increase the carbon footprint and expose the Company to stringent climate regulation, with stated negative financial implications of potential carbon taxes, compliance penalties and capital expenditure for upgrades. Evolving EPR frameworks and hazardous waste rules raise compliance requirements; management notes EPR regulations take effect from April 2026.
- Quality compliance and product rejection — MD&A 'Operational' risk: strict technical specifications across lead, copper and aluminium must be met to avoid rejections, cancellations or customer dissatisfaction. Mitigated by multi-stage quality control including microstructure and spectrometer analysis before dispatch.
- Governance / promoter regulatory exposure — BRSR Principle 1 disclosure: SEBI levied a monetary penalty in a case alleging that the Chairman and the Jain Family Trust traded shares of Refex Industries Limited while in possession of unpublished price-sensitive information under the SEBI PIT Regulations (the Company clarifies the allegations do not concern its own shares); the Securities Appellate Tribunal admitted the appeal against SEBI's order dated 12 December 2025 and stayed recovery subject to a 50% deposit. Read with the FY26 Secretarial Audit observations disclosed in the Directors' Report (sibling bundle) - a Regulation 32 deviation on IPO fund utilisation towards repayment of a promoter loan, and Regulation 23 related-party transactions with the Chairman & MD entered without prior/omnibus Audit Committee approval - this is a live governance watch-item for a company in its first year as a listed entity.
- Customer and channel concentration alongside export concentration — Structural concentration disclosed but not labelled a risk: exports are about 62% of turnover across 20 countries, and BRSR Principle 1 'Openness of business' (routed to the capex_expansion sibling bundle) shows sales to dealers/distributors at 53.33% of total sales with sales to the top 10 dealers/distributors equal to 100.00% of sales to dealers/distributors (FY25: 95.25%), across only 39 dealers. On the buy side, purchases from the top 10 trading houses were 61.23% of purchases from trading houses. [PROVENANCE: concentration figures back-filled from the capex_expansion bundle; the risks_esg bundle carries the export share only.]
- Resource management - water and process waste — BRSR material issue #6 (Risk): inefficient resource utilisation, particularly of water and process waste, threatens operational resilience, with negative financial implications from escalating water procurement costs and higher waste disposal levies. Mitigation is closed-loop water recycling systems and maximised secondary material recovery efficiency.
- Workforce composition and attrition — Structural people risk visible in BRSR Section A (routed to sibling bundles): the workforce is 443 permanent employees but 1,350 workers all of whom are 'other than permanent' (permanent workers: 0), and permanent-employee turnover was 16% in FY 2025-26 with female turnover at 36%. Board diversity is thin - 1 woman among 8 directors (12.5%) and 0 among 4 KMP. [PROVENANCE: BRSR Section A items 20-22 arrived in the profile/governance/registry bundles, not in risks_esg.]

business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body:
- Described as 'One of India's largest and fastest-growing non-ferrous metal recycling companies, with a legacy spanning over seven decades', tracing back to the 1953 partnership firm Jain Metal Rolling Mills, with operations commencing in 2013 via a lead refining unit.
- One of the largest Indian recyclers with LME-registered lead ingots (brand 'Jain 9997', registered 2022) and also registered with MCX; branded lead finished products can be sold into LME-registered warehouses to settle derivative positions.
- Six stated core competencies: strategically located multi-product recycling facilities, diversified product portfolio, customers in 20+ countries and suppliers in 120+ countries, deep sourcing capabilities, in-house tech and quality testing, and a hedging mechanism for commodity price risk.
- Customer base of 350+ with ~70% of revenue from repeat customers (FY26); top 5 customers 40.6% and top 10 51.6% of revenue, with named marquee customers including Jiangxi Copper International Trading Co. Ltd.
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Fire incident] Operations at the Unit-II facility were temporarily impacted by a fire in one of the manufacturing sheds during the quarter; after inspections and regulatory approvals, manufacturing has resumed across Unit-II excluding the affected shed, where restoration and remaining statutory compliances are progressing. Management states this has not altered long-term growth plans.
- [Discontinued operation] The 70%-owned Sharjah UAE gold refining subsidiary Jain Ikon Global Ventures (FZC), acquired in partnership with M/s Ikon Square Limited UAE and refining gold and by-product silver from August 2024, was discontinued effective 17 April 2025 (Board approval 24 August 2025) due to low margins, high operational overheads, working capital constraints and gold-refining sector volatility; it is reclassified as an asset held for disposal pending a stake divestment.
- [Regulation] Government has mandated that all new products made from non-ferrous metals must contain a minimum of 5% recycled content starting from FY28; the MoEFCC-sourced mandated recycled-content path is 5.0%, 10.0%, 15.0%, 20.0% for copper and 5.0%, 10.0%, 10.0%, 10.0% for aluminium across FY28-29E to FY31-32E.
- [Policy support] Supportive policy stack cited: Vehicle Scrappage Policy (2021), National Non-ferrous metal scrap recycling framework (2020), Steel Scrap Recycling Policy (2019), National Resource Efficiency Policy (2019), EPR framework for non-ferrous metals (2024) and National Critical Mineral Mission Policy (2025), alongside India's Rs. 1,500 crore Critical Mineral Recycling Scheme.
- [Margin commentary] Management attributes moderated margins in the quarter to the evolving product mix and the initial ramp-up of the value-added copper business, and expects sustainable margin expansion as utilization levels improve.
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: Jain Resource Recycling Limited ('JRRL') recycles and processes non-ferrous scrap - lead scrap and lead-acid batteries, copper wires, cables and scrap, aluminium scrap, tin-bearing streams and cable plastics - into refined and remelted ingots, billets, alloys and granules at integrated manufacturing facilities at Gummidipoondi, Chennai, supported by a global procurement network spanning more than 120 countries. It runs a B2B model supplying recycled non-ferrous metals and by-products to approximately 371 clients across over 20 countries, with exports contributing about 62% of total turnover; domestic marquee clients named are Vedanta, Amara Raja Batteries, Luminous Power Technologies, HBL Batteries and Chloride Metals, and international clients named are Mitsubishi Corporation, Nissan Trading, Trafigura, IXM SA, Toko Company and Hodaka. Building on this platform it is moving downstream into higher-value copper products - cathodes, wire rods and busbars.

outlook.body:
- Two-dimensional strategy stated by the Chairman & MD: grow volumes through deeper sourcing, new recycling platforms and geographic expansion, while improving profitability through value addition, better product mix and higher recovery from existing scrap streams.
- Copper forward integration as the largest and highest-priority growth vertical - moving from recycled metal to engineered products (anode, cathode, wire rod, busbar) to change the margin profile, earnings stability and customer mix towards long-term, product-specific industrial partnerships.
- Extending LME-grade credentials from lead to copper: taking the copper platform into LME-grade cathodes to create a second product stream with the same globally recognised market-access credential the lead business already enjoys.
- Lead strategy on two pillars: securing long-term raw material (25% equity stake in M/s. Abraj Al Khaleej, Kuwait, giving right-of-first-refusal access to Middle East recycled material) and progressively extracting higher value from battery scrap streams.
- Value extraction from existing scrap streams rather than new sourcing - tin recovery scaled during the year via an additional vacuum distillation furnace, with antimony extraction from lead-antimony bullion as the next unlock, positioned as an early-mover critical-mineral play aligned to the Government of India's resource security agenda.
- Decongesting plastic processing into a dedicated standalone recycling unit so plastic recycling can evolve into an independent profit centre over time.
- Securing raw material depth through the Jain CY Circular Solutions JV with C&Y Group (Ahmedabad facility) to align raw material supply with expanding downstream capability.
- Governance and risk discipline treated as strategy: structured LME hedging covering procurement and sales back-to-back within a 90-day cycle for margin visibility, plus tight working capital control, and an ongoing investment in Board, audit, internal control and disclosure standards as a newly listed company.
- Longer-term intent to enter emerging recycling verticals - tyres, end-of-life solar panels and e-waste - as those markets reach commercial scale, leveraging existing sourcing, processing, quality and risk competencies.
- Larger vision: build India's most integrated, globally connected and quality-trusted non-ferrous recycling platform, for a world where recycled materials are preferred industrial inputs rather than substitutes.
- The AR sets out a Dividend Distribution Policy (available on the Company's website under 'Investors'), but the routed text carries only the tail of that section - the visible external factors are 'statutory requirements under applicable law for the time being in force' and 'dividend payout ratios of companies in the same industry'. The internal factors and any payout guidance were cut off before the routed extract begins, so the dividend philosophy is only partially recoverable here, and no dividend recommendation, rate or payout ratio for FY 2025-26 appears anywhere in this bundle. The Company confirms there were no instances of one-time settlement with any bank or financial institution during the year. Broader capital-allocation intent must be read from sibling bundles (provenance noted): the Chairman's message states the Rs 1,250 Crores IPO comprised a Rs 500 Crores fresh issue and a Rs 750 Crores Offer for Sale, that approximately Rs 375 Crores of the fresh issue was used to prepay and repay borrowings to strengthen the balance sheet and improve financial flexibility, and that the remaining fresh-issue proceeds were directed to business expansion, working capital and operational requirements, creating headroom for capital-efficient growth investments across copper value-addition, the Ahmedabad joint venture and new processing capabilities; a CRISIL A+/Stable rating upgrade was received during the year. GOVERNANCE CAVEAT on that deployment: the FY26 Secretarial Audit recorded a Regulation 32 deviation - Rs 540 million earmarked for General Corporate Purpose was used to repay an unsecured loan to the Promoter, contrary to Prospectus disclosures, which management describes as inadvertent and temporary with the amount since returned to the Company as a loan for business purposes.
- Stated environmental pledge of 'zero discharge, zero landfill, and zero burning manufacturing', with the Company describing itself as actively decoupling growth from environmental impact (BRSR Section B item 7, Director's statement).
- Transition to renewable solar energy as the stated route to lower emissions, plus optimisation of fleet logistics as mitigation for the GHG emissions material issue.
- Proactive alignment to India's forthcoming Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regulations 'taking effect from April 2026' and to future recycled-content mandates.
- Closed-loop water recycling systems and maximised secondary material recovery efficiency as the stated mitigation for the resource-management material issue.
- Energy efficiency identified as an ESG opportunity - reducing energy intensity across processing facilities to lower utility expenditure with long-term operational savings.
- Certification stack mapped to the NGRBC principles: ISO 9001:2015, IATF 16949, ISO 14001:2015, ISO/IEC 17025:2017, ISO 45001:2018 and ISO 50001:2018.
- The business model is itself presented as the sustainability mechanism: recycled copper displacing primary copper cuts embodied energy; lead, tin and antimony recovered from end-of-life lead-acid batteries re-enter productive use; polypropylene and PVC from cable scrap are converted into RoHS-compliant granules. Power sourcing arrangements of 2.6 MW and 3 MW are disclosed for facilities.
- Community and social commitments named: elevating educational infrastructure and supporting aspiring students, empowering underprivileged women, animal welfare, and a dignified, safe and inclusive workplace. CSR is applicable under Section 135 and a CSR Committee is constituted; the CSR Policy is on the Company's website.
- Safety training reach: 1,180 worker training/awareness programmes covering 100% of workers on health and safety measures; 1,180 awareness programmes for value chain partners on safety training covering 100% of partners by value of business. Board of Directors training coverage was 25% (2 programmes) and KMP coverage was Nil.
- MATERIAL ABSENCE - NO ESG TARGETS: BRSR Section B item 5 ('Specific commitments, goals and targets set by the entity with defined timelines, if any') and item 6 (performance against them) are both answered 'NA'. Per extraction rules 'NA' is treated as UNKNOWN rather than a stated nil, but the practical position is that the AR discloses no time-bound, quantified ESG target anywhere in the routed text - the pledges above are directional only.
- MATERIAL ABSENCE - NO ASSURANCE: BRSR Section A items 14 and 15 (name of assurance provider, type of assurance obtained) are both 'NA', and Section B item 11 confirms 'No' independent assessment/evaluation of the working of its policies by an external agency. [PROVENANCE: items 14-15 arrived in the profile/governance/registry bundles.]
- MATERIAL ABSENCE - NO BOARD SUSTAINABILITY COMMITTEE: BRSR Section B item 9 answers 'No' to whether the entity has a specified Committee of the Board/Director responsible for decision making on sustainability issues; the highest authority for the BR policies is the Board of Directors, and NGRBC review frequency across all principles is 'Need-based' rather than periodic.
- POLICY GAP - PRINCIPLE 7: the entity's policies do not cover NGRBC Principle 7 (responsible public policy advocacy); the stated reason is that it 'is planned to be done in the next financial year'. Principle 9's policy is also recorded as not Board-approved, and Principles 8 and 9 policies do not extend to value chain partners.

A formal Anti-Bribery, Corruption and Anti-Money Laundering Policy, a Data Protection/IT Systems policy, a Whistle-Blower policy with the Audit Committee Chairperson as Ombudsman, a Board Diversity Policy and an ESG Policy are in place. [PROVENANCE: recall/data-breach and ABC policy detail arrived in the governance_entities and capex_expansion bundles.]

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: JRRL's expansion programme in FY 2025-26 is built around copper forward integration, raw-material security and by-product value extraction. Copper anode production commenced in March 2026 at Jain Green Technologies Unit 3, marking entry into value-added copper manufacturing; a second furnace in an advanced stage of installation is to take total anode capacity to 1,600 MT per month by Q1 FY 2026-27. Civil construction of the cathode facility is complete, with Phase 1 and Phase 2 commissioning targeted for Q2 and Q3 FY 2026-27 respectively, and wire rod and busbar commissioning following in August and September 2026; management expects the integrated platform to lift copper segment EBITDA margins by approximately 200-400 basis points. On sourcing, the Jain CY Circular Solutions joint venture with C&Y Group Investments Inc. will run an Ahmedabad facility planned to process 72,000 MT of scrap annually and generate approximately 25,000 MT of copper output per annum - factory premises finalised on lease, implementation underway, operations phased from September 2026. In lead, a 25% equity stake in M/s. Abraj Al Khaleej, Kuwait gives right-of-first-refusal access to Middle East recycled material and is expected to be operational through FY 2026-27, with minor timeline slippage attributed to shipping-route disruption. By-product value extraction advanced on two fronts: tin recovery capacity was raised from 125 MTPA to 500 MTPA during the year after installing an additional vacuum distillation furnace, and a proposed antimony extraction plant (estimated capex approximately Rs 20 Crores) is targeted for commissioning in Q3 FY 2026-27. A dedicated standalone plastic recycling unit of approximately six acres, estimated capex Rs 15 Crores, is also slated for Q3 FY 2026-27 commissioning to decongest plastic processing and turn it into an independent profit centre. The Directors' Report frames the same programme as 'strengthening its presence in the downstream metals segment through expansion into higher-value products, including copper cathodes, wire rods, and busbars', from integrated facilities at Gummidipoondi, Chennai. Environment-linked capex during the year comprised the installation of a Primary and Secondary Air Pollution Control System for the Rotary Furnace to reduce emissions and improve ambient air quality (BRSR Principle 2). NOTE ON THAT BRSR ROW: it reports environment/social capex as 0.31% of total capex for FY 2025-26 (FY 2024-25: Nil) but the Company's own footnote immediately contradicts the number - 'The Company has not separately tracked the percentage of R&D and capital expenditure investments attributable to environmental and social impact initiatives. Accordingly, the percentage is reported as NR I.E., Not Recorded.' The 0.31% is therefore not relied on and is not carried into capex_disclosed (it is also a percentage, not a rupee quantum, and did not arrive under a NAMED DISCLOSURE heading).
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Recycling moving 'from choice to necessity': non-ferrous demand rising across electrification, power, infrastructure, mobility, electronics, data centres and industrial manufacturing while primary production stays energy-intensive and mining-dependent, making secondary metals a practical alternative - JRRL says it is addressing this by expanding recycling scale across copper, lead, aluminium, tin and plastics.
- Copper demand structurally expanding on electrification, renewables, grid expansion, EVs, electronics, data centres and industrial automation, with secondary copper gaining share as a lower-carbon alternative - the stated rationale for JRRL's anode/cathode/wire rod/busbar integration.
- Formalisation of Indian recycling under recycled-content mandates, EPR frameworks and stricter environmental requirements, which management says favours organised players with compliance and traceability capability - and which is strengthening JRRL's domestic sourcing.
- Rising customer requirements for purity, consistency, traceability and delivery reliability are raising entry barriers - addressed through the global sourcing network, quality systems, LME-registered lead brand, MCX recognition, in-house processing and hedging framework.
- India emerging as a global metal recycling hub on processing capability, skilled labour, industrial ecosystems, growing domestic demand and port connectivity; the Chairman adds that India pairs a booming domestic non-ferrous consumption curve with highly optimised processing costs, a scrap ecosystem moving from unorganised to formal, strict EPR implementation, and connectivity to Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern and global trade routes.
- Critical minerals and battery recycling as an expanding opportunity, with India seeking domestic resource security - JRRL's lead recycling experience and multi-metal capability positioned to benefit.
- Erosion of virgin metal economics (energy intensity, resource depletion, tightening environmental approvals, logistics bottlenecks, shifting geopolitical alliances) is said to have carved out a distinct premium for recycled, traceable, lower-carbon secondary metals.
- Margin mechanics management flags: in sharp LME up-cycles the industry's formula-based pricing compresses realisations as a percentage of LME; combined with a spike in freight/logistics costs from geopolitical disruption to shipping routes, this temporarily compressed Q4 EBITDA margin - management states both factors were external, non-recurring and have normalised since the start of FY 2026-27.
- Sourcing mix shift: domestic sourcing strengthening as India's EPR-driven formalisation accelerates, reducing dependence on long-lead-time imports (FY 2025-26 raw material sourcing split disclosed as 39% domestic / 61% imports; revenue split 38% domestic / 62% export).
- Commissioning pipeline as the near-term earnings driver: with copper anodes live and cathodes, wire rods, busbars, the Ahmedabad JV and the plastic recycling unit all expected to commission through FY 2026-27, management expects improved product mix, deeper customer relationships, reduced earnings cyclicality and 'meaningful medium-term margin expansion'.

currentContext.expansion: JRRL's expansion programme in FY 2025-26 is built around copper forward integration, raw-material security and by-product value extraction. Copper anode production commenced in March 2026 at Jain Green Technologies Unit 3, marking entry into value-added copper manufacturing; a second furnace in an advanced stage of installation is to take total anode capacity to 1,600 MT per month by Q1 FY 2026-27. Civil construction of the cathode facility is complete, with Phase 1 and Phase 2 commissioning targeted for Q2 and Q3 FY 2026-27 respectively, and wire rod and busbar commissioning following in August and September 2026; management expects the integrated platform to lift copper segment EBITDA margins by approximately 200-400 basis points. On sourcing, the Jain CY Circular Solutions joint venture with C&Y Group Investments Inc. will run an Ahmedabad facility planned to process 72,000 MT of scrap annually and generate approximately 25,000 MT of copper output per annum - factory premises finalised on lease, implementation underway, operations phased from September 2026. In lead, a 25% equity stake in M/s. Abraj Al Khaleej, Kuwait gives right-of-first-refusal access to Middle East recycled material and is expected to be operational through FY 2026-27, with minor timeline slippage attributed to shipping-route disruption. By-product value extraction advanced on two fronts: tin recovery capacity was raised from 125 MTPA to 500 MTPA during the year after installing an additional vacuum distillation furnace, and a proposed antimony extraction plant (estimated capex approximately Rs 20 Crores) is targeted for commissioning in Q3 FY 2026-27. A dedicated standalone plastic recycling unit of approximately six acres, estimated capex Rs 15 Crores, is also slated for Q3 FY 2026-27 commissioning to decongest plastic processing and turn it into an independent profit centre. The Directors' Report frames the same programme as 'strengthening its presence in the downstream metals segment through expansion into higher-value products, including copper cathodes, wire rods, and busbars', from integrated facilities at Gummidipoondi, Chennai. Environment-linked capex during the year comprised the installation of a Primary and Secondary Air Pollution Control System for the Rotary Furnace to reduce emissions and improve ambient air quality (BRSR Principle 2). risks.note: MD&A 'Market and Financial' risk: fluctuations in global market prices for lead, copper and aluminium directly impact revenue and gross margins. Mitigation is a disciplined LME hedging mechanism with sales prices monitored against raw-material procurement. The structural exposure is visible in management's own Q4 commentary (sibling bundles): a short-window surge in LME copper compressed realisations because the industry's formula-based pricing expresses price as a percentage of LME.

risks.risk: Raw material insecurity - dependence on scrap availability
risks.note: MD&A 'Operational' risk: dependence on scrap availability, both domestic and imported, heightens sensitivity to supply-side disruption, quality variation, logistics delays and price volatility. Mitigated by a diversified sourcing network; domestic sourcing was raised to approximately 39% of volume during the year to cut dependence on long-lead-time imports. The remaining ~61% import dependence is the structural residue.

risks.risk: Foreign exchange exposure
risks.note: MD&A 'Market and Financial' risk: significant international trade in US Dollars and Euros creates currency risk. Managed by monitoring net exposures and using forward contracts, with a partial natural hedge to the extent import and export flows align.

risks.risk: Operational safety in molten-metal and hazardous-material handling
risks.note: MD&A 'Operational' risk and the top-ranked BRSR material issue: recycling, smelting, refining and handling of molten metals are safety-sensitive; recycling operations involve heavy machinery and hazardous materials posing injury risk to the workforce. Stated financial implication is negative - potential medical compensation, legal costs and operational downtime. Mitigated by safety policies, risk assessments, safety manuals, PPE, mandatory training and ISO 45001:2018 certification.

risks.risk: Geopolitical instability, shipping-route and trade disruption
risks.note: MD&A 'Strategic and External' risk: conflicts, trade policy changes, port disruptions or restrictions in key sourcing and export regions can affect procurement, logistics and market access. This risk has already crystallised twice in the year on management's own account - a freight/logistics cost spike on import containers, and delay to the Kuwait (Abraj Al Khaleej) project timeline.

risks.risk: Working capital intensity
risks.note: MD&A 'Financial' risk: timely scrap procurement, inventory holding, receivables management and funding support are critical in a volatile commodity environment. Managed through internal controls, treasury processes and management review. Structurally amplified by global sourcing, commodity-linked pricing and the working-capital-intensive nature of recycling.

risks.risk: Environmental and EPR regulatory compliance, and GHG/energy intensity
risks.note: MD&A 'Regulatory and ESG' risk (mitigation text TRUNCATED mid-sentence at 'The Company' in the routed extract) plus BRSR material issue #2: energy-intensive recycling processes increase the carbon footprint and expose the Company to stringent climate regulation, with stated negative financial implications of potential carbon taxes, compliance penalties and capital expenditure for upgrades. Evolving EPR frameworks and hazardous waste rules raise compliance requirements; management notes EPR regulations take effect from April 2026.

risks.risk: Quality compliance and product rejection
risks.note: MD&A 'Operational' risk: strict technical specifications across lead, copper and aluminium must be met to avoid rejections, cancellations or customer dissatisfaction. Mitigated by multi-stage quality control including microstructure and spectrometer analysis before dispatch.

risks.risk: Governance / promoter regulatory exposure
risks.note: BRSR Principle 1 disclosure: SEBI levied a monetary penalty in a case alleging that the Chairman and the Jain Family Trust traded shares of Refex Industries Limited while in possession of unpublished price-sensitive information under the SEBI PIT Regulations (the Company clarifies the allegations do not concern its own shares); the Securities Appellate Tribunal admitted the appeal against SEBI's order dated 12 December 2025 and stayed recovery subject to a 50% deposit. business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Jain Resource Recycling Limited ('JRRL') recycles and processes non-ferrous scrap - lead scrap and lead-acid batteries, copper wires, cables and scrap, aluminium scrap, tin-bearing streams and cable plastics - into refined and remelted ingots, billets, alloys and granules at integrated manufacturing facilities at Gummidipoondi, Chennai, supported by a global procurement network spanning more than 120 countries. It runs a B2B model supplying recycled non-ferrous metals and by-products to approximately 371 clients across over 20 countries, with exports contributing about 62% of total turnover; domestic marquee clients named are Vedanta, Amara Raja Batteries, Luminous Power Technologies, HBL Batteries and Chloride Metals, and international clients named are Mitsubishi Corporation, Nissan Trading, Trafigura, IXM SA, Toko Company and Hodaka. Building on this platform it is moving downstream into higher-value copper products - cathodes, wire rods and busbars.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Recycling moving 'from choice to necessity': non-ferrous demand rising across electrification, power, infrastructure, mobility, electronics, data centres and industrial manufacturing while primary production stays energy-intensive and mining-dependent, making secondary metals a practical alternative - JRRL says it is addressing this by expanding recycling scale across copper, lead, aluminium, tin and plastics.
- Copper demand structurally expanding on electrification, renewables, grid expansion, EVs, electronics, data centres and industrial automation, with secondary copper gaining share as a lower-carbon alternative - the stated rationale for JRRL's anode/cathode/wire rod/busbar integration.
- Formalisation of Indian recycling under recycled-content mandates, EPR frameworks and stricter environmental requirements, which management says favours organised players with compliance and traceability capability - and which is strengthening JRRL's domestic sourcing.
- Rising customer requirements for purity, consistency, traceability and delivery reliability are raising entry barriers - addressed through the global sourcing network, quality systems, LME-registered lead brand, MCX recognition, in-house processing and hedging framework.
- India emerging as a global metal recycling hub on processing capability, skilled labour, industrial ecosystems, growing domestic demand and port connectivity; the Chairman adds that India pairs a booming domestic non-ferrous consumption curve with highly optimised processing costs, a scrap ecosystem moving from unorganised to formal, strict EPR implementation, and connectivity to Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern and global trade routes.
- Critical minerals and battery recycling as an expanding opportunity, with India seeking domestic resource security - JRRL's lead recycling experience and multi-metal capability positioned to benefit.
- Erosion of virgin metal economics (energy intensity, resource depletion, tightening environmental approvals, logistics bottlenecks, shifting geopolitical alliances) is said to have carved out a distinct premium for recycled, traceable, lower-carbon secondary metals.
- Margin mechanics management flags: in sharp LME up-cycles the industry's formula-based pricing compresses realisations as a percentage of LME; combined with a spike in freight/logistics costs from geopolitical disruption to shipping routes, this temporarily compressed Q4 EBITDA margin - management states both factors were external, non-recurring and have normalised since the start of FY 2026-27.
- Sourcing mix shift: domestic sourcing strengthening as India's EPR-driven formalisation accelerates, reducing dependence on long-lead-time imports (FY 2025-26 raw material sourcing split disclosed as 39% domestic / 61% imports; revenue split 38% domestic / 62% export).
- Commissioning pipeline as the near-term earnings driver: with copper anodes live and cathodes, wire rods, busbars, the Ahmedabad JV and the plastic recycling unit all expected to commission through FY 2026-27, management expects improved product mix, deeper customer relationships, reduced earnings cyclicality and 'meaningful medium-term margin expansion'.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: JRRL's expansion programme in FY 2025-26 is built around copper forward integration, raw-material security and by-product value extraction. Copper anode production commenced in March 2026 at Jain Green Technologies Unit 3, marking entry into value-added copper manufacturing; a second furnace in an advanced stage of installation is to take total anode capacity to 1,600 MT per month by Q1 FY 2026-27. Civil construction of the cathode facility is complete, with Phase 1 and Phase 2 commissioning targeted for Q2 and Q3 FY 2026-27 respectively, and wire rod and busbar commissioning following in August and September 2026; management expects the integrated platform to lift copper segment EBITDA margins by approximately 200-400 basis points. On sourcing, the Jain CY Circular Solutions joint venture with C&Y Group Investments Inc. will run an Ahmedabad facility planned to process 72,000 MT of scrap annually and generate approximately 25,000 MT of copper output per annum - factory premises finalised on lease, implementation underway, operations phased from September 2026. In lead, a 25% equity stake in M/s. Abraj Al Khaleej, Kuwait gives right-of-first-refusal access to Middle East recycled material and is expected to be operational through FY 2026-27, with minor timeline slippage attributed to shipping-route disruption. By-product value extraction advanced on two fronts: tin recovery capacity was raised from 125 MTPA to 500 MTPA during the year after installing an additional vacuum distillation furnace, and a proposed antimony extraction plant (estimated capex approximately Rs 20 Crores) is targeted for commissioning in Q3 FY 2026-27. A dedicated standalone plastic recycling unit of approximately six acres, estimated capex Rs 15 Crores, is also slated for Q3 FY 2026-27 commissioning to decongest plastic processing and turn it into an independent profit centre. The Directors' Report frames the same programme as 'strengthening its presence in the downstream metals segment through expansion into higher-value products, including copper cathodes, wire rods, and busbars', from integrated facilities at Gummidipoondi, Chennai. Environment-linked capex during the year comprised the installation of a Primary and Secondary Air Pollution Control System for the Rotary Furnace to reduce emissions and improve ambient air quality (BRSR Principle 2). NOTE ON THAT BRSR ROW: it reports environment/social capex as 0.31% of total capex for FY 2025-26 (FY 2024-25: Nil) but the Company's own footnote immediately contradicts the number - 'The Company has not separately tracked the percentage of R&D and capital expenditure investments attributable to environmental and social impact initiatives. Accordingly, the percentage is reported as NR I.E., Not Recorded.' The 0.31% is therefore not relied on and is not carried into capex_disclosed (it is also a percentage, not a rupee quantum, and did not arrive under a NAMED DISCLOSURE heading).

one-line thesis: Jain Resource Recycling delivered record FY26 growth with 48% revenue and 56% PAT growth, driven by scale and hedging discipline, but Q4 EBITDA per ton was temporarily compressed by $4K copper LME volatility and $6K logistics shocks; management has fixed the formula mechanism and is now executing $120Cr capex to integrate copper anode/cathode/wire rod/busbar production, transforming earnings from cyclical recycling to stable value-added margins.
financial scorecard: revenue: +48% YoY (INR9,543Cr); EBITDA/margin: +53% YoY to INR559Cr (5.9% margin); PAT (rptd): +56% YoY to INR347Cr; PAT (normalized): +56% YoY (no material distortions); order book: N/A (no formal order book); net debt: INR375Cr IPO proceeds used to repay debt, leverage maintained healthy
guidance: revenue growth: double-digit (copper >15%, lead 10-15%); margin: normalized EBITDA per ton copper INR30K-32K/ton; order inflow: none specified; capex/commissioning: INR115-120Cr in FY27, with cathode (Q2FY27), wire rod (Aug26), busbar (Sep26), Ahmedabad (Dec26), Kuwait (post-shipping normalization), plastic plant (Q3FY27)
segment / subsidiary detail: Copper & alloys: 55% of revenue; Lead & alloys: 40%; Aluminium: 5%; Exports: 62%; Domestic: 38%
growth verticals / optionality: Copper cathode/wire rod/busbar integration; Antimony recovery from lead scrap; Dedicated plastic recycling unit; Kuwait JV for Middle East scrap access; Potential expansion into other specialty metals
margins & cost dynamics: Q4 FY26 EBITDA per ton copper compressed by INR18.5K due to LME formula volatility and INR6K due to shipping/logistics; normalized EBITDA per ton copper guidance: INR30K-32K; cost normalization expected in Q1FY27
capex / expansion: INR115-120Cr in FY27: Copper cathode phase 2 (INR40Cr est.), Ahmedabad JV (INR30Cr), Kuwait JV (INR30Cr), plastic recycling plant (INR15Cr), antimony recovery (INR20Cr)
capital allocation: INR375Cr of INR500Cr IPO proceeds used for debt repayment; remaining INR125Cr for capex and corporate purposes; no dividend policy disclosed; focus on capex-funded value-addition over buybacks
risks & watch-items: Geopolitical shipping disruptions (Iran/Strait of Hormuz); copper LME volatility (mitigated by new hedging mechanism); project execution delays; raw material sourcing concentration in transshipment hubs (UAE); antimony recovery tech risk
management quality / tone: Confident, forward-looking, disciplined; acknowledged Q4 headwinds as transitory; emphasized structural shift from recycling to integrated value chain; proactive on hedging reform and capex execution
non-obvious takeaways: Copper formula volatility is a market-wide phenomenon (not company-specific), akin to oil refining margins; plastic recycling is purely byproduct-driven (no virgin plastic); Kuwait project is critical for lead scrap security, not just copper; antimony recovery is a high-margin specialty metal play hidden in lead recycling
